1.pericope_label: Through desire a man, having separated himself, seeketh and intermeddleth with all wisdom
debates: Whether the separated man of the first verse is praised or blamed
Whether the third verse speaks of a person coming or of consequences following
Whether the man of the fourth verse must be supplied as wise
outliers: Clarke sets out five renderings of the first verse from the versions and older English Bibles and leaves the reader to judge
Henry takes the two similitudes of the fourth verse to be elegantly transposed, so that the spring is the deep water and the words the flowing brook
themes: One verse read as praise by some and as rebuke by others
Separation from the world and separation from other men
Understanding sought for itself or for display
Speech figured as water that does not run dry

5.pericope_label: The words of a talebearer are as wounds, and they go down into the innermost parts
debates: Whether the words of the talebearer are wounds or dainty morsels
What the mouth of the fool calls for
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch reject four proposed meanings for the word at the eighth verse as all without support
Clarke illustrates the sweetness of slander from gilded gingerbread and sweetmeats coloured with red lead
themes: The merits of a cause set against the person of a party
A quarrel entered by choice
Words that seem to grieve and secretly rejoice
Poison taken because it has been sweetened

9.pericope_label: The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe
debates: What the name of the Lord stands for
What the word rendered conceit means
How far slackness is like waste
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch reject the renderings of every translator from the Greek down to the later versions on the word at the eleventh verse
Henry says that before destruction men are commonly made more haughty than ever, so that the ruin may be the sorer
themes: Neglect counted with active destruction
A tower entered by faith
A wall that is high only in the mind
Pride and humility taken as forerunners

13.pericope_label: The spirit of a man will sustain his infirmity; but a wounded spirit who can bear?
debates: Whether the gift of the sixteenth verse is a bribe or a liberality
What the change of gender at the fourteenth verse marks
outliers: Ellicott expressly excludes the spirit crushed by the sense of sin from the wounded spirit, since God will lift that one up
Keil and Delitzsch deny that the word for gift here carries the sense of a bribe
themes: Answering before hearing
A mind that carries the body until it is itself broken
Knowledge sought by those who have it already
A door opened by a present

17.pericope_label: He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him
debates: Which reading the nineteenth verse should follow
Who the mighty of the eighteenth verse are
What the belly of the twentieth verse stands for
outliers: Henry proposes that the lot might still be used to decide controversies, if it were done with prayer and due solemnity
Keil and Delitzsch reject the reading almost all the versions agree in at the nineteenth verse, which Clarke adopts
themes: One tale good until another is told
A quarrel ended by an appeal outside itself
Brothers harder to reconcile than enemies
Words returning upon the speaker

21.pericope_label: Death and life are in the power of the tongue; there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother
debates: Whether the word good is to be supplied at the twenty-second verse
What it is to love the tongue
Whether the friend of the last verse is Christ
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch reverse the received sense of the last verse, making the man of many friends come off a loser
Clarke denies that the closing clause has any reference to God or to Christ
themes: A faculty that carries both death and life
A proverb the versions could not leave unqualified
Poverty that teaches entreaty and wealth that teaches roughness
Friendship that must be cultivated to be kept
